newsitem.title: USA: Groups baulk at Senate subpoenas in funds probe.
newsitem.headline: Groups baulk at Senate subpoenas in funds probe.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
The Senate committee investigating campaign fund raising is meeting resistance from some of the non-profit groups it has subpoenaed, which say the panel has exceeded its democratic rights.
The Senate Government Affairs Committee recently issued subpoenas to 26 organizations for documents and records relating to the 1994-1996 period.
The committee was investigating possible illegal or improper fund raising in the 1996 election campaign, with particular emphasis on the role of foreign money.
But some members would like to expand the probe to encompass the role of so-called issue advocacy groups which have been increasingly active in political campaigns.

The 26 groups which received subpoenas include 14 generally aligned with Republicans, such as the Christian Coalition, the Heritage Foundation and the National Right to Life Committee. The other 12 generally support Democrats and include the AFL-CIO labor federation, the Sierra Club and the National Education Association.

James Bopp, legal counsel to the anti-abortion National Right to Life Committee, this week sent a confidential memorandum to the other groups which received subpoenas, both of the left and right, setting out his concerns.

"The subpoenas, on their face, are astonishing in their breadth, seeking to investigate legal and constitutionally protected legislative lobbying activity and issue advocacy," he wrote in the memorandum, which was obtained by Reuters.

"The subpoenas, on their face, encompass a vast universe of documents that could not ordinarily be forced into public view. They intrude deeply into the realms of confidential communications of citizen groups," Bopp wrote.
Attorneys representing the AFL-CIO this week wrote to the committee objecting to its subpoena.

"The document subpoena directed to the AFL-CIO goes far beyond even the most generous interpretation of the committee's mandate," wrote attorneys Robert Weinberg and Robert Muse, counsels to the labor federation.
"That subpoena is a virtually unlimited search mission through almost every aspect of the AFL-CIO's operations," they wrote.
The attorneys said many of the documents had nothing to do with politics and many were sensitive or confidential.

The committee has no obligation to keep material produced in compliance with subpoenas confidential. In fact, many documents have been cited and distributed to the media and the public in committee hearings.

"As a general matter in a democracy neither the legislative nor the executive branch has a license to rummage through all the papers of individuals or their associations," the AFL-CIO attorneys wrote.
The subpoenas demand all records including financial reports, internal communications, electronic mail, working papers, drafts, letters and diaries.
A committee aide said officials had held talks with about a dozen of the 26 organizations to limit the scope of the subpoenas and planned to meet with several more.
"We are willing to work with them to protect their interests, in a way that is consistent with the need for the committee to conduct the investigation," he said.

Some members of the committee have themselves objected to scope of the subpoenas. Democrats and Republicans have repeatedly wrangled about subpoenas, each accusing the other side of seeking to harass organizations engaged in legitimate political activity.
But senators on the panel appeared to strike a political compromise on subpoenas last month to avoid the committee becoming paralyzed by partisan bickering.

Each side essentially agreed to allow the other virtual free rein in the issuance of subpoenas, with Republicans targeting groups that support Democrats while Democrats focusing on Republican backers."
